newsitem.title: LITHUANIA: U.S., Russia want framework arms deal this month.
newsitem.headline: U.S., Russia want framework arms deal this month.

text.p: The United States and Russia have agreed to seek an extension of current talks on updating a European conventional arms treaty in a bid to reach a framework agreement by the end of July, U.S. officials said on Sunday.

The officials were speaking as U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright travelled to the Lithuanian capital Vilnius for a meeting with Baltic foreign ministers after talks in St Petersburg with Russian Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov.
The current round of Conventional Forces in Europe (CFE) talks, grouping 30 nations in Vienna, is due to end shortly, but Russia and the United States want to speed up the pace.

A senior U.S. official said Albright and Primakov "agreed to jointly recommend to the negotiators in Vienna to stay in session till the end of the month to see if their efforts could yield a framework agreement for an amended CFE treaty".

The original treaty, signed in 1990, set limits on the tanks, artillery pieces, aircraft and other non-nuclear arms that European states could hold, but needs revision because of major political changes on the continent since then.
Russia is worried that NATO plans to admit former Warsaw Pact countries could endanger its security and until recently was insisting that old "bloc" limits on arms holding should continue to apply.
Western officials say they want to assure Moscow that "an enlarged NATO will not pose an enlarged threat" but are unwilling to give Russia a veto over the arms of new NATO members.
The U.S. official said Albright and Primakov made no breakthrough on the substance of the talks but agreed to send more experts to Vienna to boost the negotiating effort.

He said the two were expected to meet again in Kuala Lumpur on or around July 24 at a meeting of Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) foreign ministers and could if necessary try then to clinch an outline deal.

NATO is keen to allay Moscow's concerns following its decision at a summit in Madrid last week to invite Poland, the Czech Republic and Hungary to apply for membership, a move strongly criticised by the Kremlin.

Albright's trip to Vilnius is aimed, by contrast, at assuring the former Soviet Baltic states of Lithuania, Latvia and Estonia that they too will have a chance at some future date to apply for NATO membership.
In St Petersburg, Albright told Russians firmly on Sunday that the Baltic states could not be excluded from entry despite Moscow's fierce opposition to former Soviet republics joining the alliance.
"We have said all along that NATO is open to all democratic market systems in Europe," Albright said in a Russian television interview.
"All those kind of countries are eligible. It doesn't matter where a country is on the map, they are eligible for membership in NATO," she said.

Although the NATO summit mentioned the Baltic states favourably, it gave no assurances on when they might be able to apply to join, unlike Romania and Slovenia which received strong hints they might form the second wave of entrants.

The Baltic states were incorporated into the Soviet Union during World War Two and became independent in 1991. Still fearful for their freedom, the three countries are anxious to gain NATO protection.

But Russia, which has grudgingly accepted the expansion of the alliance into Central Europe, has said it may tear up a recently signed charter of cooperation with NATO if former Soviet republics are admitted to the alliance.

After five hours in Vilnius, Albright was to travel on Sunday evening to the Czech Republic, the land of her birth. The highlight was to be an emotional trip to Prague's Jewish cemetery to look at records of her grandparents who, it was recently disclosed, died in the Nazi holocaust.
